title: Weekly resistance-training volume and muscle growth (dose-response)
summary: A meta-analysis showing a graded dose-response between weekly set volume per muscle and hypertrophy.
claims: Higher weekly set volume per muscle group is associated with greater muscle hypertrophy in a dose-response manner.
Roughly 10 or more hard sets per muscle group per week tends to maximize hypertrophy for most trainees.
Adding sets generally adds growth up to a point, after which recovery becomes the limiting factor.

title: Dietary protein and resistance-training adaptations
summary: A meta-analysis on protein supplementation and resistance-training-induced gains in strength and mass.
claims: Protein intakes around 1.6 g per kg of bodyweight per day maximize resistance-training-induced gains in lean mass.
Intakes beyond roughly 2.2 g/kg/day provide little additional benefit for muscle growth.
Total daily protein matters more than precise per-meal timing for hypertrophy.

title: Resistance-training frequency and hypertrophy
summary: Evidence on how often to train a muscle per week when volume is equated.
claims: When weekly volume is equated, training a muscle group twice per week is at least as effective as once per week for hypertrophy.
Higher frequencies can help distribute volume into more productive, less fatiguing sessions.
Frequency is mainly a tool to accumulate weekly volume with good per-set quality.

title: Inter-set rest intervals for strength and hypertrophy
summary: A study comparing short vs longer rest periods on muscular adaptations.
claims: Resting about 2-3 minutes between sets supports greater strength and hypertrophy than very short (~1 minute) rest.
Longer rest preserves per-set performance, allowing more total quality volume.
Compound lifts benefit most from longer rest intervals.

title: RPE and reps-in-reserve for autoregulated training
summary: Framework for using rating of perceived exertion and reps-in-reserve to autoregulate load.
claims: Rating sets by reps-in-reserve (RIR) lets lifters autoregulate load to daily readiness.
Most hypertrophy work is effective in the range of roughly 0-4 reps in reserve.
Autoregulating with RPE helps manage fatigue across a training block.

title: Proximity to failure and muscle growth
summary: A meta-analysis on how close to failure sets must be taken for hypertrophy.
claims: Training close to failure drives hypertrophy, but sets do not have to reach absolute failure.
Stopping a few reps short of failure produces similar growth with less fatigue.
Reserving 1-3 reps lets you accumulate more weekly volume sustainably.

title: Load and repetition ranges for strength vs hypertrophy
summary: Evidence on heavy vs moderate loads for different adaptations.
claims: Hypertrophy is similar across a wide range of loads when sets are taken near failure.
Maximal-strength gains are greater with heavier loads (roughly 1-6 reps).
Train heavy for strength specificity and use moderate reps to accumulate volume comfortably.

title: Progressive overload as the driver of adaptation
summary: Position stand emphasizing progression of training stimulus over time.
claims: Continued progress requires progressively increasing the training stimulus over time.
Overload can be added via load, reps, sets, or improved technique and range of motion.
Small, consistent increments are more sustainable than large jumps.

title: Fatigue management and deloads
summary: On managing accumulated fatigue to sustain long-term progress.
claims: Planned reductions in volume or intensity (deloads) help dissipate accumulated fatigue.
A stalled or declining estimated 1RM can signal accumulated fatigue rather than lost strength.
Periodically reducing volume can restore performance and allow further progress.

title: Periodization for strength development
summary: Meta-analysis comparing periodized vs non-periodized training.
claims: Periodized resistance training produces greater strength gains than non-periodized training.
Varying intensity and volume across a block manages fatigue and drives progress.
Both linear and undulating periodization outperform constant programming for strength.

title: Sleep extension and athletic performance
summary: Sleep extension improved performance metrics in athletes.
claims: Extending sleep improves reaction time, mood, and physical performance in athletes.
Inadequate sleep impairs recovery and training readiness.
Prioritizing sleep is a high-leverage recovery intervention.

title: Energy availability for muscle gain
summary: On energy balance requirements for gaining lean mass.
claims: A modest caloric surplus supports muscle gain while limiting fat gain.
Trained lifters gain muscle slowly, so an aggressive surplus mostly adds fat.
Adequate energy and protein together drive lean-mass accrual.

title: Repetition tempo and muscular adaptations
summary: Review of lifting tempo and time-under-tension on growth.
claims: Very slow lifting tempos are not superior and can reduce the volume you can perform.
A controlled eccentric (lowering) phase is sufficient to stimulate growth.
Extremely long reps mainly reduce total work without extra benefit.

title: Exercise selection and variation
summary: On varying exercises to develop a muscle more completely.
claims: Some exercise variation can promote more complete muscle development.
Excessive novelty undermines progressive overload and skill in key lifts.
Keep core lifts stable to track progress, and rotate accessories.
